THOUGHT: The patient reports ~2 months of classic early-pregnancy symptoms (breast tenderness, nausea, urinary frequency, weight gain) and believes she is pregnant, but objective testing does not support pregnancy. A urine β-hCG was negative and transvaginal ultrasound showed no gestational sac. Urine pregnancy tests are generally sensitive to ≥~25 mIU/mL; by ~5 weeks gestational age a transvaginal ultrasound will usually visualize a gestational sac once serum β-hCG is >~1500–2000 mIU/mL. Given the duration of symptoms (≈2 months), a true intrauterine pregnancy large enough to produce detectable hCG and a sac would be expected; ectopic pregnancy and molar pregnancy are unlikely with a negative β-hCG and normal pelvic exam/US. A chemical pregnancy (very early loss) could cause a transient positive hCG followed by decline, but the current negative urine test and absent sac argue against an ongoing pregnancy. The constellation of persistent pregnancy-like signs and symptoms in the absence of biochemical or sonographic evidence of pregnancy — coupled with a strong desire/expectation to be pregnant — is most consistent with pseudocyesis (false pregnancy). Clinical next steps (not requested but relevant) would include obtaining a serum β-hCG to definitively exclude very low-level/early pregnancy and providing sensitive counseling and psychological support; evaluate for alternative medical causes of symptoms (thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia) as indicated.

DIAGNOSIS: Pseudocyesis (false pregnancy).
